stem.text: Bromine reacts with ethene in the dark.
Which description of the organic intermediate of this reaction is correct?

explanation.text: This is electrophilic addition. The C=C electrons induce a dipole in Br<sub>2</sub>, attack the δ+ Br atom and the Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically, giving Br<sup>–</sup> and the carbocation CH<sub>2</sub>Br–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>.
The carbocation has a positive charge and an empty orbital, so it accepts a lone pair from Br<sup>–</sup> in the second step. A species that accepts an electron pair is an electrophile.

optionAnalysis.text: The intermediate is a carbocation, so it is positively charged. The negative species formed is Br<sup>–</sup>, which is not organic.
In the dark there is no UV light to cause homolytic fission, and the mechanism is ionic; free radicals belong to free-radical substitution of alkanes.
The carbocation is attacked by the nucleophile Br<sup>–</sup>; it does not donate an electron pair itself.
CH<sub>2</sub>Br–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> has a positive carbon that accepts an electron pair from Br<sup>–</sup>, so it is an electrophile.

reasoningChain: Br<sub>2</sub> + ethene in the dark: electrophilic addition, ionic mechanism.
It accepts an electron pair from Br<sup>–</sup>: an electrophile.

inferredMistakes.text: Thinking that because Br<sub>2</sub> is the electrophile, the intermediate it forms must be a nucleophile.
Associating bromine with free radicals from alkane substitution, ignoring that the reaction is in the dark.
